author: Deeg
name_in_asr: Andaluo 案達羅 (*ʔanh-dat-la, Āndhra); capital Pingqiluo 瓶耆羅 (*bεjŋ-gji-la, Skt. *Veṅgi(pu)ra)
asr_identification: Veṅgīpura = the excavated site of Peddavegi, between the Krishna and Godavari, c. 10 km N of Eluru, Andhra Pradesh
evidence: Reconstructs 瓶耆羅 as *Veṅgi(pu)ra; Xuanzang does not transcribe pu- although he regularly writes -pura as 補羅 (Siṃhapura, Ānandapura), so the form he heard may have lost the p (Mizutani: Telugu *veṅgiura). For the site he cites Subramanian 1932 and Sarma 2002: Peddavegi excavated and identified, its earliest stratum relatively late (4th/5th c.). His own reading of the account: the capital is named for Andhra but not for Dhānyakaṭaka, perhaps because Xuanzang took the capital's name for the kingdom's.
quote: He gives the name of the capital of Āndhra as Pingqiluo 瓶耆羅 / *bεjŋ-gji-la, Skt. *Veṅgi(pu)ra…Excavated and identified as the archaeological site of Peddavegi, between the Krishna and Godavari rivers about 10km north of Eluru, with a relatively late earliest stratum dated to the 4th / 5th cent.
note: Agrees with the study and Mizutani (capital Veṅgī at Peddavegi, high). Adds only the transcription argument for the missing -pura; no new site evidence. His 'earliest stratum 4th/5th c.' understates the 2nd–3rd-c. Brāhmī finds the study cites (IAR 1986–87; cf. Francis in griffiths2025_earlyandhradesa:1).

author: Deeg
name_in_asr: Āndhra and Great Āndhra (大安達邏) / Dhānyakaṭaka; the new capital Veṅgīpura
asr_identification: political and religious centre shifted from the lower Krishna (Dhānyakaṭaka) to the Godavari side (Veṅgīpura, inland between the rivers)
evidence: Reading of the two country entries against the epigraphic record: Andhra proper has 20 monasteries and 3,000 monks and a prominent monastery of the arhat Acala; Dhānyakaṭaka many deserted monasteries, 20 inhabited, 1,000 Mahāsāṅghika monks and 100 deva temples. Deeg takes this to show a decline of Buddhism in the south and a shift of the centres to Veṅgī, which he finds consistent with the post-Ikṣvāku inscriptions (Śālaṅkāyanas to Viṣṇukuṇḍins, the latter ruling until some decades before Xuanzang).
quote: Overall, Xuanzang’s report implies a shift of the political and religious centres from the area around the banks of the Krishna River to the Godavari River…The fact that the new capital Veṅgīpura was located inland between the two rivers may indicate a decline of economic activities along the coastline
note: Agrees with the study's division (10.13 at Peddavegi; 10.14 on the Krishna). Context only: a deserted southern country under Veṅgī's shadow suits the study's point that nothing yet shows the Dharanikota town standing in the 7th c.; no site evidence.

author: Deeg
name_in_asr: Tuonajiezhejia 馱那羯磔迦 (*da-na’-kɨat-trε:jk-kɨa, *Dhānakaṭaka), also 大安達邏; Shugu 熟穀 'Ripe Grain' (Mahāmeghasūtra)
asr_identification: Dhānyakaṭaka = Amaravati (Ray 1986) or more precisely Dharanikota, W of Amaravati on the S bank of the Krishna (Shimada 2013)
evidence: Name: na 那 cannot stand for Skt. nya or MIA ña, so Xuanzang's form is *Dhānakaṭaka. Location only by reference (Ray; Shimada 2013: 36, 38). Adds the Mahāmeghasūtra prophecy (Dharmakṣema, dated 417; T.387): in the small kingdom 無明 (Āndhra, from andha 'blind') a city 熟穀 on the S bank of the river 黑闇 (Kṛṣṇā), Lévi's dhānya-; the Prakrit Dhaññakaḍa is now attested in the Kanaganahalli inscriptions.
quote: In this kingdom there is a river called “Black,” [and] on its southern shore there…Already Lévi made the very plausible suggestion that the city name Shugu 熟穀, “Ripe Grain,” has to do with Skt. dhānya…or more specifically with Dharanikota, a site west of Amaravati on the southern bank of the Krishna, see Shimada 2013
note: Agrees with the study (Dharanikota, medium). The Mahāmeghasūtra passage is the one Ji already cites (after Takakuwa) for a city on the S bank; Deeg gives the full text and translation. No new site evidence.

author: Deeg
name_in_asr: Fuposhiluo 弗婆勢羅 (Pūrvaśaila, 東山); Afaluoshiluo 阿伐羅勢羅 (*ʔa-bat-la-ɕiajh-la, avara-, 西山)
asr_identification: not located; the two convents named after the Pūrvaśaila and Aparaśaila subgroups of the Mahāsāṅghikas, attested in Andhra inscriptions
evidence: Xuanzang's two convents bear the names of two Mahāsāṅghika subgroups, 'confirmed by the epigraphic evidence'. Tournier (to Deeg): Andhra inscriptions write apara-, with one exception, EIAD 55, where the lineage receiving the land grant is Avara(ddāra)seliya; Xuanzang's 阿伐羅 likewise points to avara. The description of the convents (dam on the river, cut cliffs, galleries) is close, partly verbatim, to that of Bhramaragiri (10.12.05). His translation swaps the glosses (弗婆勢羅 'Western', 阿伐羅勢羅 'Eastern Mountain'), a slip against the Chinese he prints (東山/西山).
quote: in the inscriptions from Āndhra the first part of the compound is generally apara, with a single important exception (eiad 55), where the monastic lineage benefitting from the land-grant is called Avara(ddāra)seliya. Xuanzang’s transcription interestingly suggests avara
note: No location; does not touch the study's open verdicts. The avara- form ties Xuanzang's name to EIAD 55, the Patagandigudem plates granting land to a monastery at Piṭhuṇḍa, which the volume places perhaps near Guntupalli in the Godavari–Krishna doab (griffiths2025_earlyandhradesa:5), not W of Dharanikota.

author: Deeg
name_in_asr: Baluomoqili 跋邏末羅耆釐 (Bhramaragiri, 黑蜂); king Suoduopohe 娑多婆訶 (Sātavāha(na)) and Nāgārjuna
asr_identification: not located; the Nāgārjuna–Sātavāhana legend attached to a monastery N of Andhra (Xuanzang's Kosala)
evidence: Textual: Xuanzang alone connects Nāgārjuna with Bhramaragiri, while most evidence ties Nāgārjuna to Andhra; Tournier asks whether the legacy of Nāgārjuna's monastery was transferred from Andhra to a well-known monastery further north. Deeg: a king Sātavāha(na) had very likely already been linked with Nāgārjuna and with a region further north (Kosala) rather than with Andhra. The Andhra convents' description repeats that of Bhramaragiri.
quote: As it is only Xuanzang connecting Nāgārjuna to the Bhramaragiri monastery while most of the evidence points to Āndhra, is it possible that the legacy of the monastery of the famous master was transferred from Āndhra to another well-known monastery further to the north?
note: Bears on the Nāgārjunakoṇḍa/Śrīparvata candidate (Mizutani's, uncertain): on this reading the Nāgārjuna association of Xuanzang's mountain is a legend moved north, not a pointer to Nāgārjunakoṇḍa, which is consistent with the study keeping Bhramaragiri in Kosala (Arang, low). Does not locate the mountain.

author: Deeg
evidence: Name only: of the possible forms only Coliya is attested, e.g. in Pāla inscriptions (Tournier to Deeg).
quote: 珠利耶 / *tɕuă-lih-jia, Skt. *Colya / *Culya / Coliya; Vincent Tournier reminds me that only this last form of the name is attested, for instance in Pāla inscriptions.
note: Agrees with the study's name note (Coḷiya, three syllables, against Mizutani's culya) and adds Pāla attestations of the form; does not bear on Nellore vs Cuddapah.

author: Deeg
name_in_asr: 孤山; Chenna 陳那 (*Diṇṇa, Dignāga)
evidence: Translation and notes on the Dignāga passage (name *Diṇṇa, the gloss 童授 a confusion with Kumāralāta); nothing on the hill's location.

author: Deeg
name_in_asr: 大山巖, Asura palace of Popifeijia 婆毗吠伽 (Bhāviveka)
evidence: Translation of the Bhāviveka legend with notes (Eckel's comparison with Mahākāśyapa waiting for Maitreya); nothing on the hill's location.

author: Deeg
name_in_asr: Azheluo 阿折羅 (所行) arhat's great monastery and stone stūpa near Pingqiluo
evidence: Name only: the arhat is Acala (Buddhabhadra's inscription in Ajanta cave XXVI, Tournier 2020), Xuanzang's *Ācala a corrupt form; against ācāra (Ji, Mizutani). Not located.
note: Place missing from the table: the monastery of the arhat Acala beside the capital of 10.13. See griffiths2025_earlyandhradesa:2 for a site proposal.

author: Francis (in Griffiths, Tournier & Shimada eds.)
name_in_asr: Vijayaveṅgīpura / Vijayaveṅgī (Śālaṅkāyana charters); Pingqiluo 瓶耆羅; Bēnagouron (Ptolemy)
asr_identification: Veṅgīpura = Peddavegi near Eluru (Ellore), Eluru district, Andhra Pradesh: 'very plausible' but without hard proof
evidence: Seven of the ten Śālaṅkāyana inscriptions are issued from Vijayaveṅgīpura, two from Vijayaveṅgī (EIAD 159–168); Ptolemy's Bēnagouron of the Salekēnoi above the Maisōloi (Masulipatnam) is taken as Veṅgīpura; Samudragupta's 'Hastivarman of Veṅgī'. Hultzsch (1908) identified Peddavegi from a mound the villagers called the temple of Citrarathasvāmin, the plates of EIAD 165 found in nearby Kolleru lake, and Elūra of EIAD 159 = Eluru, 7 mi away. Sarma's excavations (2002) confirm early importance (brick stūpa of phase IA, 4th–5th c.; Viṣṇukuṇḍin temples) but yielded 2nd-c. inscriptions and no Śālaṅkāyana inscription or coin, nor the Citrarathasvāmin temple. Veṅgī was conquered by the Viṣṇukuṇḍins c. 450 (EIAD 180).
quote: Veṅgī has been identified, as we have just seen, as the Bēnagouron of Ptolemy, but also as one of the Āndhra places visited by Xuanzang…But it remains puzzling that the site has yielded early inscriptions of the 2nd c. ce (Sarma 1987), but no Śālaṅkāyana inscriptions or coins…The identification Peddavegi with the Veṅgī of Śālaṅkāyanas remains very plausible, but we do not have any hard proof of it, only serious hints.
note: Agrees with the study (Peddavegi) but tempers it: the editor of the Śālaṅkāyana charters finds no inscription or coin of the Veṅgī kings at the site and calls the identification very plausible, not proven. The study's 'high' rests on the excavated fortified city of Xuanzang's period, not on a name; this supports noting that nothing on the site names Veṅgī (as the note already says).

author: Francis (in Griffiths, Tournier & Shimada eds.)
name_in_asr: big monastery near Pingqiluo with a stone stūpa 'several hundred feet high' (Acala's monastery); Mahānāgaparvata = Guntupalli
asr_identification: perhaps the Buddhist complex at Guntupalli (ancient Mahānāgaparvata), Eluru district, Andhra Pradesh; tentative, no definitive identification
evidence: Guntupalli excavated (Sarma 1988): stūpas, a pillared maṇḍapa, an apsidal shrine and vihāras, rock-cut and brick, some from the 2nd c. BCE; inscriptions earlier than the Śālaṅkāyanas (EIAD 203–219) name the place Mahānāgaparvata; EIAD 164 (Śālaṅkāyana Nandivarman II) on a pillar at the stūpa site near the caves; a bronze with the ye dharmā stanza in Nāgarī (EIAD 219), 6th–10th c. (9th c., Sarma). Francis thinks Xuanzang's description may be of Guntupalli by someone who had only heard of it, but too vague to decide.
quote: This might be a description of Guntupalli, by someone who did not actually visit the spot but had heard of it. In any case, the description is so vague that it does not seem possible to propose a definitive identification.…Inscriptions earlier than the Śālaṅkāyanas (eiad 203–219) were found, which name the place Mahānāgaparvata.
note: New candidate for a place missing from the table (Acala's monastery beside the 10.13 capital). Site evidence for Guntupalli as a long-lived monastery, but nothing names Acala and the text puts the monastery 'beside the city, not far' (瓶耆羅城側不遠), while Guntupalli lies some 40 km N of Eluru in the hills; the Aśoka stūpa SW of it and Dignāga's hill 20 li SW would follow. Alternative, low.

author: Singh; Ollett, Tournier & Griffiths; Gillet (in Griffiths, Tournier & Shimada eds.)
asr_identification: Dhānyakaṭaka = Dharanikota near Amaravati, Guntur (Palnadu) district, Andhra Pradesh; a royal headquarters under the Ikṣvākus
evidence: EIAD 20 (Nāgārjunakoṇḍa, Bodhisirī) records a stone maṇḍapa at a vihāra at Dhaññakaḍa, glossed 'mod. Dharanikota near Amaravati' (Singh); the nigama of Dhānyakaṭaka gives at Amaravati, and Dhaññakaṭa supplies most donors at Kanaganahalli. The Patagandigudem plates of Ehavala Cāntamūla (EIAD 55, 3rd c.) are issued from the 'victorious royal headquarters' of Dhaññakaḍa (Tournier, via Gillet). Memorial pillars from Dharanikota (to c. 300): EIAD 568, a Tamil Brahmin mahāgāmika shown before a king; EIAD 622, a mahāraṭṭhi's daughter; EIAD 564 (field E of Dharanikota), an amātya's wife; EIAD 586, 625.
quote: a stone maṇḍapa at a vihāra at Dhaññakaḍa (mod. Dharanikota near Amaravati)…this copper-plate grant was issued from the “victorious royal headquarters” of Dhaññakaḍa (Dhānyakaṭaka, associated with Amaravati)…there is another remarkable memorial from Dharanikota, close to Amaravati
note: Agrees and adds evidence (study: Dharanikota, medium): the name Dhaññakaḍa as a royal seat under the Ikṣvākus and memorials of officials and a king's court at Dharanikota itself. All of it is 3rd c. or earlier; nothing of the 7th-c. city, so the rating stays medium.

author: Kieffer-Pülz; Singh (in Griffiths, Tournier & Shimada eds.)
asr_identification: a locality Puvasela in Bodhisirī's list of donations, not necessarily at Nāgārjunakoṇḍa: the list may run from local sites downstream along the Krishna
evidence: EIAD 20, line 3 (Nāgārjunakoṇḍa): gifts at eleven places, among them 'at the Eastern Mountain (puvasele) a pond and a veranda and hall', a stone pavilion at the E gate of the mahācetiya at Kaṇṭakasola (= Ghantasala, c. 220 km E of Nāgārjunakoṇḍa), and (Tournier's new reading of §11) a stone pavilion at a monastery at Dhaññakaḍa. Hence the monasteries need not lie at Nāgārjunakoṇḍa; Tournier suggests the list starts with local sites and then goes downstream along the Krishna (perhaps from Devagiri on). Puvvaseliya monks are attested in EIAD 49, 100, 200 (Alluru and the lower Krishna).
quote: 6 puvasele taḷākaṁ aḷaṁdāmaḍavo ca at the Eastern Mountain a pond and a…This identification implies that the monasteries enumerated in eiad 20 need not be situated in Nagarjunakonda but may also lie in the surrounding or in some more distant areas…the list starts with local sites before going downstream along the Krishna
note: Bears on the study's open verdict: the Puvasela of the Nāgārjunakoṇḍa record (Vogel's locality there) may lie down the Krishna, not at Nāgārjunakoṇḍa, and Dhaññakaḍa is listed separately, so the record does not put an 'Eastern Mountain' at Dharanikota either. 3rd c.; does not locate Xuanzang's convent. Stays open.

author: Strauch; Kieffer-Pülz (in Griffiths, Tournier & Shimada eds.)
name_in_asr: Piṭhuṁḍa / Pithudu(pura), mahāvihāra of the Avara(ddāra)seliyas (EIAD 55); Aparaśailas at Ghantasala and Pedavegi (EIAD 100, 594)
asr_identification: Aparaśaila houses in the Krishna–Godavari region: Piṭhuṇḍa perhaps at or near Guntupalli, Eluru district (Subrahmanyam, Strauch), near Amaravati not excluded; Ghantasala; Pedavegi
evidence: The Patagandigudem plates (EIAD 55, Ikṣvāku Ehavala Cāntamūla, last quarter of the 3rd c.) grant land to the mahāvihāra at Piṭhuṇḍa (Kieffer-Pülz), the lineage being Avara(ddāra)seliya (Tournier, in Deeg). Strauch: Pithudu is also named on a Vaddamanu potsherd ('resident of Pithudu town'); the plates were found at Kallacheruvu, W of Rajahmundry, c. 10 km from Guntupalli, so Pithudu may be at or near Guntupalli; Ramachandra Murthy's site near Amaravati not excluded. Kieffer-Pülz: the Ghantasala monastery likely Aparaśaila (EIAD 100 reading), as suggested by EIAD 594 from Pedavegi, which names Kaṇṭakasola and reads a(pa)rasel-.
quote: According to these plates, Piṭhuṁḍa was the site of a mahāvihāra.…It is therefore tempting to accept Subrahmanyam’s hypothesis and to locate ancient Pithudu at or near the Buddhist site Guntupalli in the Eluru district of Andhra Pradesh.…The affiliation to the Aparaśailas is suggested by eiad 594 from Pedavegi
note: Bears on the study's note (Shimada's Pithunda 'north of Dhāṃñakaṭaka'): the only avara- record names a monastery perhaps c. 90 km NE, in the doab near Guntupalli, and other Aparaśaila traces are at Ghantasala and Pedavegi; none lies W of Dharanikota. Shows the sect in the region, not the western convent; unlocated, low, as the study has it.

author: Singh (in Griffiths, Tournier & Shimada eds.)
asr_identification: Amaravati great stūpa, Guntur (Palnadu) district: Buddhist inscriptions continue into the 5th–9th and 10th–14th c.
evidence: Of the Amaravati inscriptions, three belong to the 5th–9th c. (Sivaramamurti 1942 nos. 123, 124 = EIAD 423, 424; Sewell 1880 = EIAD 138) and six to the 10th–14th c. (Hultzsch; EIAD 574, 624); a 12th-c. inscription on an Amareśvara temple pillar records a land grant for the mahācaitya; a Sinhalese inscription at Gadaladeniya records a Sri Lankan monk's gifts at Amaravati; Amaravati continued till the 14th c.
quote: the Buddhist epigraphic record at Amaravati continues into later centuries—three inscriptions belong to the 5th–9th centuries,41 and six to the 10th–14th centuries.
note: Site evidence of some Buddhist activity at the Amaravati stūpa around Xuanzang's time (none dated closely). Xuanzang says the eastern convent had stood empty for over a century; if the stūpa was still receiving gifts in the 5th–9th c., this adds a small difficulty for Amaravati = Pūrvaśaila, beside Shimada's 'on a plain'. Alternatives stay open.
